rationale: Evidence from iteration 5 (score 371.0): the oval completes in 20/20 trials (progress 0.998, mean 2.01 s, rms 0.017), so the baseline tracking is sound. The s-bend (progress 0.26) and slalom (progress 0.16) still leave the course in every trial. max_error sits at the 0.06 m off-track floor while rms_error is only about 0.028, so the robot is drifting steadily outward on bends rather than oscillating. Line loss is essentially absent on the s-bend. Body width cannot widen the limit (0.0125 + 0.18/4 = 0.0575 is still below the 0.06 floor), so the fix must come from the controller and dynamics. Iteration 5's wider 7-sensor span with matched kp (5.3) helped slalom progress (0.10 to 0.16) and s-bend progress slightly (0.23 to 0.26), which suggests sensing is no longer the main limit. My working hypothesis is that at base_speed 0.85 (about 1.7 m/s) the drive wheels slip on the tighter bends, so the robot understeers outward even though the steering command is correct. Changes: (1) base_speed 0.85 to 0.75 to reduce lateral slip demand on bends. The oval has about 1 s of margin, and at 2.0 s it should still finish near 2.4 s. (2) kd 0.7 to 0.8 to add damping, since the higher effective gain and lower speed may leave the response a little underdamped. (3) mass 0.42 to 0.40, the minimum, to reduce yaw inertia slightly. Geometry sensors, kp 5.3, ki 1.0, wheel_track 0.08 and line_loss last_direction are unchanged, so the speed and damping effect is isolated. Hypotheses: (a) s-bend progress rises above 0.4 with the slip reduction; (b) the oval still completes in at least 80% of trials; (c) steering_oscillation stays below about 0.3 with the higher kd. If the s-bend still drifts out at lower speed, the next lever is ki or kp, not speed. If the oval fails to finish, speed must come back up to about 0.8. Expected result: fewer off-track exits on the s-bend and slalom, with the oval completing.
